Due dates and payment in halves

The full bill is due on or before December 20 of the levy year. Owners who prefer can pay in two halves: the first by December 20, and the second by June 20 provided the first half was paid in full (Idaho Code 63-903).

Partial payments are accepted whenever you make them. They do not wipe out costs, interest or late charges that already accrued, though. Whatever is left of the first half after December 20 picks up late charges and interest, and the second half does the same after June 20.

A missed or subsequent roll works differently. The tax collector has 30 days after the roll arrives to send the bill, and payment is still due by June 20. After that date the tax is delinquent. A second, unexpected bill on a parcel you are selling is worth a call to the county treasurer to find out if it comes from a missed roll.

The valuation date for your house

Idaho values taxable property as of 12:01 a.m. on January 1 of the year the tax is levied. Real, personal and operating property are all assessed annually at market value as of that moment (Idaho Code 63-205).

Why this matters at sale time: a house that sells in October is still taxed on how it stood the previous January 1. Work done or damage suffered after that date leaves the current bill unchanged. If a house burned or was gutted in the spring and the roll still shows the old condition, take it to the county assessor, and act fast, because appeal windows are strict.

Idaho keeps the assessor, who sets value, separate from the treasurer, who bills and collects. Calls about value go to the first office. Calls about balances, payoff figures and payment history go to the second.

What a late payment costs

Interest on a delinquency is charged at one percent per month, counted from January 1 following the year the tax lien attached. Interest is not charged on collection costs (Idaho Code 63-1001). Late charges apply on top of interest under section 63-201.

Collected late charges and interest go to the county auditor, who splits them among the taxing districts in proportion to each district's share of the tax. Paying current taxes does not stop a delinquency proceeding already under way for an earlier year (Idaho Code 63-903(7)).

Interest on a balance missed at the December 20 deadline begins the following January 1. The rate is monthly, so a full year of delay means twelve months of it, before late charges and costs. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff figure for the day you plan to close, because the number moves every month.

Idaho property tax dates at a glance

County offices can add local rules, so confirm dates with your treasurer and assessor.

EventDate or rule
Valuation date12:01 a.m., January 1 of the levy year
Tax due in full, or first halfDecember 20
Second half dueJune 20 of the following year
Interest on delinquency1% per month from January 1 after the lien attaches
Property Tax Reduction application (2027 taxes)January 1 to April 15, 2027
Property Tax Deferral application (2027 taxes)January 1 to September 7, 2027
Tax deed to the countyNot redeemed within 3 years of delinquency

Programs that lower or delay a home's property tax

The State Tax Commission and county assessors run three homeowner programs. Every one requires its own application, and all sit beside the homestead exemption, which has a separate page.

  • Property Tax Reduction. Savings run from $250 to $1,500, applied to the home plus one acre at most. Qualifying for 2027 means 2026 income after medical expenses of $40,030 or less, plus one of these: age 65 or older, blind, widowed, disabled, a former POW or hostage, or a fatherless or motherless child under 18. File annually from January 1 through April 15. Approval shows as a credit on the December bill.
  • Property Tax Deferral. Taxes on the house and up to an acre are put off, with the tax and interest repaid later. The 2027 income ceiling is $63,400 and the filing window is January 1 to September 7. The state pays the county directly, so your bill shows no deferral.
  • Disabled Veteran benefit. A veteran rated 100% service-connected disabled can see tax cut by as much as $1,500, regardless of income. Filing runs January 1 to April 15 as well.

Fees that local governments charge for solid waste, irrigation and the like are not reduced by any of these programs. A seller who used deferral owes that money back, so check with the assessor on how the balance gets handled before closing.

When an owner stops paying for years

If delinquent real property is not redeemed within three years of the delinquency date, the county tax collector must make a tax deed to the county (Idaho Code 63-1005). The county cannot take the deed until it has given notice of the pending issue and recorded an affidavit of compliance.

The notice rules are specific:

  • Record owners and parties in interest get notice by certified mail with return receipt, sent between five months and two months ahead of the planned deed date.
  • A published notice must run weekly for four straight weeks, and the final run must come at least 14 days before the deed date.
  • Each notice names the owner, describes the parcel, gives the delinquency year, itemizes the amount owed, and states when and where the deed will issue.
  • At least five working days before issuance, the tax collector signs an affidavit of compliance and has it recorded with the county recorder.

Record owners also pay the costs of preparing, serving and publishing the notice, and those costs become a perpetual lien in favor of the tax collector. Even after a tax deed issues, the record owner or a party in interest may still redeem until the county commissioners enter into a contract of sale (Idaho Code 63-1007).

Selling an Idaho house with tax still due

Unpaid property tax does not block a sale. Closing proceeds normally cover the balance. The steps are short, and the order matters.

  1. Request a written payoff from the county treasurer listing each delinquent year, interest and costs, with a good-through date.
  2. Look for any year close to the three-year mark. A parcel nearing a tax deed has a hard deadline that outranks any closing date.
  3. Hand the payoff figure to the title or escrow company so it can be paid out of the proceeds.
  4. Ask the assessor about any homestead exemption, deferral or reduction on the parcel before you transfer.

Timing can trip up a closing. In Kootenai County, escrow may not pay the treasurer when closing falls before annual tax information is available or before the second installment is due, and then the buyer or seller is left holding the credit. Wherever the house is, ask the title company how current-year taxes will be prorated and who actually sends the payment.

Owners with an exemption problem have one more reason to act early. When a house goes to a bona fide purchaser for value before a notice of intent to attach a lien for an improperly claimed exemption is recorded, the assessor and treasurer stop recovering that unpaid amount (Idaho Code 63-602G). The buyer is protected, so clean up any exemption issue before listing.

A cash sale has no lender underwriting or appraisal, so the title work and the payoff set the schedule. Get the tax figure first and the rest tends to follow.

Frequently asked questions

When are Idaho property taxes due?

December 20 for the whole bill. Owners can split it, paying the first half by December 20 and the second by June 20 of the next year, as long as the first half is paid in full.

How much interest does Idaho charge on late property tax?

One percent per month, counted from January 1 following the year the lien attached, plus late charges. Interest is not charged on collection costs.

Can I sell my Idaho house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. Closing proceeds normally pay off the tax, interest and costs. Request a written payoff from the county treasurer and hand it to the title or escrow company.

Does Idaho have help for seniors or disabled homeowners with property tax?

Yes. Property Tax Reduction can lower tax by $250 to $1,500 for qualifying owners, the Disabled Veteran benefit can reduce it by up to $1,500, and Property Tax Deferral lets qualifying owners postpone tax, which must be repaid later with interest.

How long before a county can take a house for unpaid property tax?

Three years from the delinquency date. If the parcel is still not redeemed, the tax collector must issue a tax deed to the county after proper notice and a recorded affidavit of compliance.

Two kinds of homestead protection in Idaho

Idaho uses the word homestead for two different protections, and sellers often mix them up. One is a property tax exemption on an owner-occupied home. The other is a debt protection that shields part of a home's equity from creditors.

The tax exemption lives in Idaho Code 63-602G and is applied by your county assessor. The creditor protection lives in Idaho Code title 55, chapter 10. Each has its own dollar limit, its own rules and its own effect when you sell, so they are covered separately below.

ProtectionStatuteAmountWhat it does
Homeowner's (tax) exemption63-602GLesser of $125,000 or 50% of assessed market valueLowers the taxable value of the home
Judicial homestead55-1003 and 55-1008Up to $175,000Protects equity from attachment, execution or forced sale for the owner's debts

How much the tax exemption is and who qualifies

The exemption removes the first $125,000 of market value, or 50% of market value if that is less, from property taxation. It covers your home and up to one acre of land. The cap was $100,000 in 2019 and 2020 and has been $125,000 from 2021 through 2025.

The home must be owner-occupied and be your primary dwelling place. The statute defines that as the single place where you have your true, fixed and permanent home and to which you intend to return when you are away. Under Idaho Code 63-701, the homestead is the dwelling plus the land around it that is reasonably necessary for use as a home, up to one acre.

  • You certify to the county assessor that you are applying and that the home is your primary dwelling.
  • You certify that you have not applied in another county or for another homestead in the same county.
  • A home with a multipurpose office still qualifies, but any part used exclusively for something other than the owner's dwelling does not.
  • An owner can also be a beneficiary of a trust, or a partner, member or shareholder of an entity that holds title, if proof is provided as the statute describes.

Applications ask for your full name, date of birth, current address and previous address, plus an Idaho driver's license or ID number. A new Idaho resident who lacks one has 90 days after the initial application to supply it.

When and how to apply

You apply once, through the county assessor, and the application has to be in by the last business day of the year to get the exemption for that tax year. The full exemption takes effect as of January 1 of the tax year in which a complete application is submitted and approved. It is not prorated.

Approved applications received after the second Monday in July are granted as tax cancellations for the amount of the exemption the property qualified for, which is a different path from an application filed before that date.

You do not reapply each year as long as you still occupy the same homestead as your primary dwelling. Each county assessor prescribes the form, so ask that office which one to use.

What happens to the exemption if you sell, rent out or inherit the home?

The exemption depends on the owner living in the home, so it does not pass to the next owner automatically. The one-time application only holds while the same owner still occupies the same homestead. A buyer who plans to live in your house should expect to file on their own.

Renting the house changes things. The statute requires owner occupancy as the primary dwelling, with a specific carve out for owners away on active military service whose homes are leased. Those owners must apply every year by a deadline the county assessor sets, and the county may discontinue the exemption if they miss it.

When an owner dies, the exemption continues for the year of death and the following tax year as long as the home remains part of the estate. After that, the new owner must reapply and meet the qualification rules. If you are selling an inherited house, that gives the estate a limited window before the tax bill reflects the loss of the exemption. Our Idaho probate guide explains how estates handle the sale itself.

Penalties for claiming more than one homestead

Claiming more than one homestead exemption triggers recovery of tax for up to seven years plus a penalty. The county assessor investigates before granting the exemption and must refuse it if it appears to be improperly claimed. If an improper claim turns up later, the assessor decides whether it should have been allowed and, if not, notifies the taxpayer in writing and assesses a recovery.

  • The recovery equals the exempted value times that year's levy, for each year of improper claiming up to seven years, plus costs, late charges and interest.
  • On a first discovered instance of claiming more than one exemption, a penalty equal to the recovered tax is added.
  • A later violation within seven years of that instance is a misdemeanor under the statute.
  • You can appeal the refusal, the recovery or the penalty to the county Board of Equalization within 30 days of the assessor's notice.

Unpaid recovered tax becomes a lien on the real property, and the assessor records a notice of intent to attach a lien 30 days after notifying the taxpayer. If the property is sold to a bona fide purchaser for value before that notice is recorded, the county stops recovering the unpaid amount. If you moved and claimed a new homestead after January 1, the exemption on the old property comes off the following tax year, so tell both assessors when you sell.

How the judicial homestead protects equity when you sell

Idaho law exempts the homestead from attachment and from execution or forced sale for the owner's debts, up to $175,000. Idaho Code 55-1003 sets that cap regardless of the lot's area. Section 55-1008 adds that the proceeds of a good faith voluntary sale made to acquire a new homestead, and insurance proceeds held to restore or replace the home, are exempt for one year from receipt, up to the same amount.

Sellers should plan around that one-year rule. If you sell and intend to buy another house, keep the proceeds identifiable and move quickly. The new homestead acquired with the proceeds is also exempt. If you do not buy a replacement within the year, the protection for the cash may lapse.

Section 55-1008 begins with the words "except as provided in section 55-1005," so the protection has exceptions. Talk to an Idaho attorney before closing on a house if you have judgments or large unsecured debts.

Other Idaho property tax relief that touches a sale

The homeowner's exemption is the base, and two other programs build on it. The Property Tax Reduction program can cut taxes by $250 to $1,500 on the home and up to one acre. You apply every year between January 1 and April 15, and the property must have a current homeowner's exemption. Approved benefits appear on the December property tax bill.

The Property Tax Deferral program lets you postpone paying taxes on the home and up to one acre, though you must pay the taxes and interest later. To qualify for 2027, your 2026 income must be $63,400 or less, and you apply between January 1 and September 7, 2027. If you have deferred taxes and sell, expect the amount owed to come up at closing. The Tax Commission's homeowner page links each program, and the county treasurer can give you a payoff figure.

Property taxes are due December 20, with the option of paying half by then and half by June 20. If you sell mid-cycle, ask the county treasurer what has been paid and what is outstanding.

Selling for cash with a homestead exemption

A cash sale does not change your exemption rights, but it can shorten the time you carry the home and its tax bill. We buy houses as they are, and we review the property, the title and the county tax status before making an offer. We do not quote prices without seeing the house.

  1. Pull your latest assessment notice and tax bill from the county assessor and treasurer.
  2. Check whether the homeowner's exemption, reduction or deferral is active on the parcel.
  3. List liens, judgments or deferred taxes that must be cleared at closing.
  4. If you plan to buy another home, talk to an attorney about the one-year proceeds rule before you sign.

Nothing here is legal or tax advice. Statutes change, and the legislature updates its online Idaho Code each July after a session, so confirm the current text with the county office or a qualified professional.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Idaho homestead exemption?

The tax exemption is the first $125,000 of assessed market value or 50% of market value, whichever is less. The separate creditor protection under Idaho Code 55-1003 goes up to $175,000.

Do I have to reapply every year?

No, not if you still occupy the same homestead and it remains owner-occupied. You apply once with the county assessor. Owners away on active military service with a leased home must reapply every year.

What is the deadline to apply?

Apply by the end of the county's normal business hours on the last business day of the year to receive the exemption for that tax year. Approved applications received after the second Monday in July are granted as tax cancellations.

What happens to the exemption when a homeowner dies?

It continues for the year of death and the next tax year while the home stays part of the estate. After that, the new owner must reapply and meet the qualifications.

Can I claim homestead exemptions on two homes?

No. Claiming more than one triggers recovery of tax for up to seven years and a penalty equal to the recovered tax on a first instance. A later violation within seven years is a misdemeanor.

title: Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Idaho Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Estate tax and inheritance tax in Idaho

Idaho collects no estate tax or inheritance tax today. It has no gift tax either, and its estate tax expired in 2004. The estate tax rules still on file apply only to deaths before January 1, 2005.

An heir selling an Idaho house therefore owes no state death tax on the transfer itself. The State Tax Commission takes questions about deaths before 2005 at (208) 334-7660 in the Boise area and (800) 972-7660 toll-free.

Other taxes can still reach an inherited house. Very large estates face federal estate tax, a sale can create income tax on a gain, and the property tax bill keeps coming while the estate is open.

When the federal estate tax applies

Federal estate tax matters only when an estate tops the basic exclusion amount, set at $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026. A federal return is required at that same figure for the year of death.

Federal estate and gift figures for 2026
MeasureAmount (2026)
Basic exclusion amount$15,000,000
Estate tax filing threshold$15,000,000
Annual gift exclusion per donee$19,000

Confirm the amount for the year of death, since the figure is set by federal law and can change.

The test looks at the whole estate, not the house alone. An executor totals real estate, bank and brokerage accounts, business interests and other assets to decide whether a federal return is due. Most Idaho families fall well below the line.

An heir's basis when an Idaho house is sold

For tax purposes the heir's starting cost is usually the home's market value on the day the owner died (IRS Publication 551). Any gain is counted from that figure, and what the original owner paid long ago drops out.

  • A quick sale near the date-of-death value leaves little gain.
  • Holding the house while prices climb makes the rise above that value taxable.
  • A different rule can apply when the decedent was given the property within a year before death.
  • An appraisal dated to the day of death backs up the figure.

When the house later sells, our Idaho capital gains guide covers the state's 60% deduction for real property held 12 months. A tax professional can say how that 12-month clock runs for inherited property.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Idaho house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who can sell an inherited house?

Only the court-appointed personal representative can sign a sale. Under Idaho Code 15-3-711 the representative holds the same control over title that an absolute owner has, as a trustee for those entitled to the estate, and section 15-3-715 lists authorized transactions, including selling, mortgaging or leasing real or personal property of the estate.

The same section lets the representative:

  • dispose of land, in Idaho or another state, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale;
  • make ordinary or extraordinary repairs to buildings;
  • pay taxes, assessments and the costs of administration;
  • hire attorneys, auditors or agents to help.

A will or court order can narrow these powers, so a will that restricts sale changes the answer. Buyers get some cover from Idaho Code 15-3-714: a limit on the representative's power binds only people who actually knew about it.

The small estate affidavit

Idaho Code 15-3-1201 lets a successor collect certain assets by affidavit when the probate estate is worth $100,000 or less. It works once 30 days have elapsed since the death, and only if no petition for a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere.

The affidavit route reaches payment of debts, tangible personal property, instruments of debt and securities. Real estate is absent from that list, so a house is not clearly within this shortcut. Ask the title company what it needs to close, and see a probate attorney if the estate is under the threshold but holds real property.

The affidavit must state that the fair market value of the entire estate subject to probate, less liens and encumbrances, is no more than $100,000. The Department of Health and Welfare is treated as a successor for medical assistance recovery in some cases, under subsection (c). Our Idaho probate guide explains the court route in full.

Idaho statutes that govern an estate sale

Estate administration lives in Title 15, Chapter 3 of the Idaho Code, the Uniform Probate Code chapter on wills and administration. Five of its parts bear on a house sale.

  • Part 7: duties and powers of personal representatives.
  • Part 10: closing estates.
  • Part 11: compromise of controversies.
  • Part 12: collection of personal property by affidavit and summary procedure for small estates.
  • Part 13: uniform estate tax apportionment.

Part 13 only divides estate tax among recipients. It creates no state tax. Parts 7 and 10 do the most work in a sale: Part 7 sets what the representative may do, and Part 10 covers wrapping up the estate once the house has closed.

A gift during life raises a different question. Idaho has no gift tax, and the federal annual exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2026. A gift of real estate worth more than that amount is a federal question to raise with a tax professional. Our Idaho quitclaim deed guide covers the deed itself.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Idaho houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Costs while the house is unsold

From the date of death until closing, the estate carries the property tax, insurance and upkeep. Counties treat the estate like any other owner. Take Ada County: the first half falls due December 20 and the second half June 20, and a late payment draws a 2% charge plus monthly interest.

The personal representative may pay taxes and administration expenses out of estate funds under section 15-3-715. The homeowner's exemption runs until ownership changes or the home stops being a primary residence. Ask the county Assessor if it carries on after a death.

Our Idaho property tax guide and the county guides for Ada and Canyon list the assessor and treasurer offices.

Timing matters for the carrying costs. Each month the house stays unsold adds another round of utilities and insurance, so ask the title company early how long it expects to need once the court has confirmed the representative's authority.

What heirs commonly face

A vacant inherited house keeps running up tax, utility and insurance bills, and any will restriction or court order must be settled before a sale.

We buy houses as is in Idaho, including inherited ones, so cleanout and repairs do not need to come first. Call or text for a written cash offer, and if you decline it you owe us nothing. Before you accept any offer, confirm the personal representative holds the authority described above and that an attorney has looked over the estate papers.

Pull together the death certificate, the court letters, the deed and the newest property tax bill before talking to any buyer. A title company asks about those four items first.

Frequently asked questions

Does Idaho have an inheritance tax?

No. Idaho has no gift tax or inheritance tax, and its estate tax expired in 2004.

Do I owe tax when I inherit a house in Idaho?

Idaho does not tax the inheritance itself. You may owe income tax on a gain if you later sell for more than the date-of-death value.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?

The basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026, and the filing threshold is the same.

Can a personal representative sell real estate without court approval?

Idaho Code 15-3-715 lets a personal representative sell estate real property unless the will or a court order restricts it, so check both.

Is a small estate affidavit enough to sell a house?

Probably not. Idaho Code 15-3-1201 covers payment of debts, tangible personal property, instruments and securities for estates of $100,000 or less, and real estate is absent from that list.

What an Idaho quitclaim deed does

An Idaho quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer has in a property, without promising that the interest is good. It is a conveyancing instrument that makes no warranties and simply releases the grantor's current right, title and interest.

That is the whole test of when it works. The deed moves what the grantor has, and nothing more. If the grantor owns the whole house, the grantee gets the whole house. If the grantor owns half, the grantee gets half. If the grantor owns nothing, the deed passes nothing.

Between the parties the conveyance is final. A grant of an estate in real property is conclusive against the grantor and anyone who later claims under the grantor, with one exception: a purchaser or encumbrancer who acts in good faith, pays value and first duly records an instrument can come out ahead (Idaho Code 55-606). That exception is why recording matters so much, and a later section returns to it.

When a quitclaim deed makes sense

A quitclaim works best between people who already trust each other and already know the title. It is a poor fit for a sale to a stranger, because the buyer gets no promise about the title.

  • Adding or removing a spouse. A couple who own a home together can change how title is held.
  • Moving a house into a trust or an LLC. The owner and the new holder are effectively the same person or group.
  • Clearing a name from title after a divorce or a family agreement. One person releases whatever claim they have.
  • Fixing a gap. A person who may hold a stray interest signs to release it.

It works less well on the open market. A buyer using a lender will usually expect a title company to insure the title, and a bare quitclaim leaves the insurer to check everything behind it. For an heir or co-owner who wants a quick cash sale, the deed is usually one step in a longer title path, not the end of it. If you are unsure whether the person signing actually holds title, find out before the deed is signed, not after it is recorded.

What an Idaho deed must contain

An Idaho deed must be in writing, signed by the person giving up the property or an agent authorized in writing, and it must show the grantee's name and complete mailing address (Idaho Code 55-601). The mailing address is easy to forget and is a common reason a recorder questions a document.

Before recording, the signature must be acknowledged, which in practice means signing before a notary or other authorized officer. The statute lists who acknowledges for different signers: the person executing it, a corporation's officer, a partner, or a manager or member of a limited liability company. A deed signed and acknowledged in another state or country under that place's law is entitled to record, and an attached certificate of acknowledgment is prima facie sufficient (Idaho Code 55-805).

If an attorney in fact signs, the power of attorney has to be filed for record in the same office before the deed itself is recorded (Idaho Code 55-806). A quick checklist helps:

  • Grantor's signature, acknowledged
  • Grantee's full name and complete mailing address
  • A legal description of the property that matches the existing record
  • Recorded power of attorney first, if an agent signs
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Idaho house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where and how to record an Idaho deed

You record a deed with the county recorder of the county where the property sits (Idaho Code 55-808). An instrument counts as recorded when, being duly acknowledged, it is deposited with the proper officer at the recorder's office (Idaho Code 55-809).

Kootenai County shows how a local office handles it. The recorder is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding holidays, charges the standard $10 for the first page and $3 for each additional page on document types without a special rate, and sells copies of recorded documents at $1.00 per page. Other counties set their own hours and methods, so call or check the county website before sending a deed.

State law also treats instruments delivered to a county recorder as recorded rather than merely filed, except plats, surveys, corner records and Uniform Commercial Code instruments (Idaho Code 31-3205(4)).

Recording fees for deeds and related documents

Idaho sets recording fees by statute (Idaho Code 31-3205), and a deed of 30 pages or less costs $15.00 to record.

Document or serviceStatutory fee
Deeds, grants and transfers of title (30 pages or less)$15.00
Other instruments, first page$10.00
Each additional page$3.00
Reconveyance of a trust deed or release of a mortgage (30 pages or less)$15.00
Power of attorney$25.00
Substitution of trustee$10.00
Copy of a record, each page$1.00
Certificate under seal, when required$1.00
Taking an acknowledgment, including seal$1.00

These are the recorder's fees. A notary, a title company or an attorney may charge separately for their own work. A deed longer than 30 pages falls under the per-page schedule instead of the flat $15.00.

What happens if a quitclaim deed is never recorded?

An unrecorded deed still binds the people who signed it, but it leaves the new owner exposed. Idaho Code 55-815 makes an unrecorded instrument valid between the parties and those who have notice of it, while Idaho Code 55-812 makes an unrecorded conveyance void against a later purchaser or mortgagee in good faith who records first. Lease terms of one year or less are treated differently.

Recording reverses that risk. Once an acknowledged conveyance is recorded, its filing with the recorder is constructive notice of its contents to everyone (Idaho Code 55-811). Anyone who later checks the county records is treated as having been warned.

For a seller, this has a direct cost. If a family member quitclaimed a share to you and never recorded it, a buyer's title search may not show your ownership. A title company will usually want the gap cured before closing, and that can slow a sale you wanted to be quick. Record the deed as soon as it is signed and acknowledged.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Idaho houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax and a later sale after a quitclaim

A deed changes the name on title, but it does not change what is owed on the parcel. Idaho property tax is due December 20, or in halves with the second half due June 20, and the tax follows the property (Idaho Code 63-903). A new owner who receives a deed from a relative takes the parcel with whatever is unpaid.

The homestead exemption depends on the owner living in the home as a primary dwelling, and the owner certifies to the county assessor that no other homestead exemption is claimed (Idaho Code 63-602G). After a transfer, ask the assessor whether the exemption stays, ends or needs a new application.

When a quitclaim is part of a probate or family transfer and the house will be sold, line up these items first:

  • A title report showing who actually holds title today
  • The recorded deed, with its instrument number
  • A payoff figure for property tax and any loan
  • Written agreement among co-owners if more than one person must sign the sale

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a notary to record an Idaho quitclaim deed?

Yes in nearly every case. Idaho Code 55-805 requires the signer's execution to be acknowledged, or proved and certified, before an instrument can be recorded. A deed acknowledged in another state under that state's law is also entitled to record.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Idaho?

The statutory fee for a deed or transfer of title of 30 pages or less is $15.00. Notary and attorney fees are separate.

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee I own the house?

No. A quitclaim makes no warranties and releases only the grantor's current interest. If the grantor had no title, the grantee receives none.

Where do I record an Idaho deed?

With the county recorder in the county where the property is located. Idaho Code 55-808 places the record in that county.

What must the deed say about the buyer?

It must include the grantee's name and complete mailing address, and it must be in a signed writing, under Idaho Code 55-601.

How Idaho taxes gain on a house sale

Idaho includes a home sale gain in your state taxable income, and it lets you deduct 60% of the gain from qualifying Idaho property. A capital gain is what you receive for a capital asset above its cost or other basis. A gain on an asset held one year or less is short term, and a gain on one held longer is long term.

There is no separate rate. Whatever gain is left after the deduction stays in taxable income and is taxed at the single rate on Idaho taxable income, 5.3% for 2025. That rate dropped from 5.69%, effective January 1, 2025, so check the rate for the year you sell.

Federal tax is a separate layer. This page covers the Idaho side, and what Idaho starts from is the gain you report federally.

Idaho Code 63-3022H

Idaho Code 63-3022H gives an individual a deduction equal to 60% of capital gain net income from the sale or exchange of qualified property, for tax years after 2001. The statute sets the main limits:

  • The property must have had an Idaho situs at the time of sale.
  • Real property must be held at least 12 months.
  • The deduction cannot exceed the capital gain net income from all property included in taxable income.
  • Gains that the Internal Revenue Code treats as ordinary income do not qualify.
  • The deduction is reduced by any federal capital gains deduction for the same property, but not below zero.
  • Property depreciated under section 1245 is not treated as real property for the deduction.

Estates, trusts, S corporations, partnerships and LLCs can also hold qualified property, so the deduction is not limited to people selling a personal residence. Part-year and nonresident owners of multistate entities compute it under State Tax Commission rules.

Which Idaho property sales qualify?

Idaho real property qualifies once you have held it 12 months, for sales on or after January 1, 2005. Sales before that date needed 18 months. For this deduction, real property means land, and includes easements, grazing permits and other section 1250 property.

Holding periods for the 60% deduction
PropertyHolding periodQualifies?
Idaho real property12 monthsYes
Timber grown in Idaho24 monthsYes
Cattle or horses for breeding, draft, dairy or sporting use24 monthsYes
Real property outside IdahoAnyNo
Stocks, bonds, LLC or S corporation interestsAnyNo

For an installment sale, the holding-period test is the one in effect in the year of the sale, under Income Tax Administrative Rule 171.06c.

A house you owned for under a year is outside the deduction, which hits flippers and anyone who bought, repaired and resold quickly.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Idaho house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The federal home sale exclusion and Idaho

The federal exclusion lets you remove up to $250,000 of gain from income, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home as your main home for at least two of the last five years. IRS Topic 701 and Publication 523 explain the rules.

Idaho's Form CG asks for the qualifying gain from sale of a personal residence as it appears on federal Schedule D. The form's wording points to the taxable gain from the sale of your Idaho home, so the Idaho deduction would apply to the gain that remains after the federal exclusion. Confirm that treatment with a tax professional for your sale.

In short, the order runs: federal exclusion first, then Schedule D, then the 60% Idaho deduction on what is left, then the 5.3% rate on the remaining Idaho taxable income.

Forms and records to gather

Idaho requires Form CG, Capital Gains Deduction and Instructions, to compute the deduction. The form asks for a description of the property and its Idaho location, the dates acquired and sold, the sales price, cost or other basis and the gain or loss.

  • The settlement statement from the sale, to document the price and selling costs.
  • Records of your purchase price and improvements, to support basis.
  • Federal Schedule D information, since Form CG draws on it.
  • Proof of the dates you bought and sold, to show the 12-month holding period.

The Form CG page has the current form. Idaho Income Tax Administrative Rules 170 to 173 cover the deduction in general, qualified property, revenue-producing enterprises and pass-through entities.

Inherited houses and basis

Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value at the date of the decedent's death (IRS Publication 551). That can leave little gain on a house the family sells soon after the death.

If the heir sells at close to the date-of-death value, there may be little or no gain to deduct. If the house is held and appreciates before the sale, the gain above the stepped-up value is a normal capital gain, and Idaho's 60% deduction can apply once the holding period is met. There are exceptions, such as property given to the decedent within a year before death. Our Idaho estate and inheritance tax guide covers the death-tax side.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Idaho houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How the holding period is counted

Idaho borrows the federal holding-period rules in section 1223 of the Internal Revenue Code, with a few state adjustments. Time held by a corporation other than an S corporation does not count, and neither does time held in property you gave up in an exchange if that property would not have qualified.

For a house, the count usually runs from the date you acquired it to the date you sold it. The statute requires at least 12 months, so count carefully from your closing date and confirm the exact day with a tax professional. If an S corporation or an entity taxed as a partnership distributed the property to you, the time that entity held it counts toward your 12 months, whether or not the distribution was a liquidating one.

The statute covers a sale or an exchange, so a swap of real property is analyzed under the same section.

Common seller situations

Three come up often: a house sold within 12 months of purchase, a rental that was never a main home, and an owner who lives in another state. The first is a plain holding-period test. Gains that the Internal Revenue Code treats as ordinary income are also excluded.

It helps to keep the tax separate from the fees. A capital gain is reported on your income tax return, while closing costs and any back property tax come out of the proceeds at settlement. If the house needs work or carries unpaid taxes, a cash buyer can close without repairs. We buy houses as is in Idaho. Call or text for a written offer, and if you turn it down you owe us nothing.

Whichever route you take, have a tax professional run your numbers before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Does Idaho have a capital gains tax?

Idaho taxes capital gains as part of income at its regular rate, 5.3% for 2025, but allows a deduction of 60% of qualifying gain from Idaho real property held at least 12 months.

What form claims the Idaho capital gains deduction?

Form CG, Capital Gains Deduction and Instructions, computes the deduction. It includes a line for the qualifying gain from the sale of a personal residence as shown on federal Schedule D.

Does Idaho follow the $250,000 home sale exclusion?

Idaho starts from the gain reported on federal Schedule D, so gain excluded under the federal rule is not part of what Idaho taxes. Confirm the details of your case with a tax professional.

Do I owe Idaho tax if I sold a house I owned for 10 months?

The 60% deduction requires a 12-month holding period for real property, so a house held 10 months would not qualify for it.

Can an out-of-state owner use the deduction?

The property must have an Idaho situs at the time of sale. For part-year and nonresident owners of multistate entities, the deduction is computed under State Tax Commission rules.

Cash Home Buyers in Idaho

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Idaho Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Idaho House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Idaho?
We buy Idaho houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

When a house goes through probate in Idaho

Probate is the court process that moves a dead person's property to the people entitled to it. It is not a taxation process, and in Idaho it is generally needed when title to property has to be transferred.

A court decides whether a will is valid if there is one, and an inventory is made. Heirs are located, creditors are identified and paid, tax returns are filed, and title is formally transferred. Property that passes by beneficiary designation, such as life insurance proceeds and retirement plans, sits outside the probate estate.

For a house, the real question is who has legal authority to sign the deed. Until a personal representative is appointed, or another lawful transfer route is completed, an heir usually cannot sell the property alone. That is why many inherited houses sit for months before a sale.

Informal versus formal probate

Idaho has adopted the Uniform Probate Code, which makes probate simpler than in states that have not modernized their codes. A probate can be informal or formal, and either kind can be supervised or unsupervised by the court.

Probate pathHow it works
Informal probateSometimes the court can handle it without hearings, which may bring speed and simplicity
Formal probateThe court gives full attention, including a ruling on whether a will exists and who the heirs are, with full notice to interested parties
SupervisedCourt direction and protection for the personal representative
UnsupervisedNo court direction or protection for the personal representative
Summary administrationAvailable when a spouse is the beneficiary, with assets passing to the spouse on an expedited basis

Formal probate fits best when there are disputes about a will's validity or the appointment of a personal representative, questions about heirs, or challenges to distribution. Its drawbacks are time and cost. A buyer, including a cash buyer, will want to know which path your estate is on because it affects when the personal representative can sign.

Can a small estate skip probate?

Only for personal property, and only up to a limit. Under Idaho Code 15-3-1201, 30 days after death a person holding the decedent's tangible personal property or owing a debt to the decedent must deliver it to someone claiming to be the successor who presents an affidavit. The affidavit must state that the entire probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000.

  • At least 30 days must have gone by since the death.
  • No application or petition for appointment of a personal representative or for summary administration may be pending or granted in any jurisdiction.
  • The claiming successor must be entitled to the payment or delivery, including as a trust under a will.

This route reaches tangible personal property, debts, stock and similar instruments. It does not transfer real property, so a house usually needs a different path. The statute also treats the Department of Health and Welfare as a successor for recovering medical assistance, after it mails notice to known heirs, successors and creditors. If the decedent received Medicaid, ask the department how that affects the estate.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Idaho house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When the surviving spouse is the only heir

Idaho Code 15-3-1205 offers a summary administration for estates where the surviving spouse is the sole devisee or heir. The spouse, or a person claiming through the spouse, files a verified petition that states the marriage and the death. If the decedent left a will, the original must accompany the petition, and notice of hearing is given under section 15-1-401.

If the court finds that the couple were married and the spouse is the sole heir or devisee, it enters a decree with the same effect as a formal decree approving or determining distribution. The petitioner need not appear in person. The spouse or the attorney may appear by phone with a motion, or submit affidavits before the hearing certifying that notice was given and no objection was received.

There is a catch. A spouse who elects this route assumes liability for any indebtedness that could be a claim against the estate, and there is no administration of the estate. Talk to an attorney before choosing it, particularly if the decedent had unpaid medical bills or loans.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes. Idaho law lists selling estate real property among a personal representative's powers. Idaho Code 15-3-715(23) lets a personal representative sell, mortgage or lease any real or personal property of the estate, or any interest in it, for cash, credit, or part cash and part credit, with or without security for unpaid balances.

A few things have to line up before a closing. The personal representative needs a court appointment. Creditors' claims are handled under 15-3-803, which bars claims against the estate unless they are presented within the time limits it sets.

A cash sale can help an estate that has to cover debts, taxes and upkeep while the court process runs, because there is no loan approval to wait on. We make an offer only after reviewing the house, and we do not quote a price on this page.

How long you have to open a probate

Generally three years after the death. Idaho Code 15-3-108 bars any informal probate or appointment proceeding, and any formal testacy or appointment proceeding, begun more than three years after the decedent's death, with listed exceptions. It also excludes a few proceedings, such as probating a will already probated at the testator's domicile and appointments in estates with a prior appointment.

Because of those exceptions, an older estate can come out either way. If a parent died several years ago and the house was never retitled, take the facts to an Idaho attorney soon.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Idaho houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax, homestead exemption and disclosure on an inherited house

Three Idaho rules affect an estate holding a house. First, property taxes are due December 20, and the owner may pay half by December 20 and the balance by June 20.

Second, the homestead exemption continues for the year of the owner's death and the next tax year while the home remains part of the estate. After that, the new owner must reapply and qualify. Our Idaho homestead exemption guide explains the exemption.

Third, Idaho Code 55-2505 exempts some transfers from the seller property condition disclosure requirement. A transfer by a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate and a transfer from a decedent's estate are exempt. So is a transfer from someone who has not occupied the property within one year and acquired it by inheritance or devise. The exemption does not stop a buyer from inspecting the house or asking questions.

Selling an inherited house step by step

Start by confirming who has authority, then handle title and tax matters before the closing.

  1. Find the will and the death certificate, and list the decedent's assets and debts.
  2. Decide whether the estate needs informal or formal probate, or whether a spouse can use summary administration.
  3. Have the court appoint a personal representative if the sale requires one.
  4. Check the county treasurer for unpaid taxes and the assessor for the exemption status.
  5. Gather offers, including cash offers, and review them with your attorney.
  6. Close, record the deed at the county recorder's office, and distribute proceeds as the court or the will directs.

The Court Assistance Office has a statewide help line at 208-746-7541, and the Idaho State Bar runs a lawyer referral service. This page is general information, not legal advice.

Frequently asked questions

Do you need probate to sell a house in Idaho?

Usually yes, unless the house passes outside probate or a spouse uses summary administration. The small estate affidavit in Idaho Code 15-3-1201 covers personal property, not real property, so a house generally needs a personal representative or another lawful transfer.

What is the Idaho small estate limit?

$100,000. Under 15-3-1201, the probate estate less liens and encumbrances must not exceed that amount, and at least 30 days must have gone by since the death.

How long do I have to start probate in Idaho?

Generally within three years after the death under Idaho Code 15-3-108, with listed exceptions. Ask an attorney if the death was several years ago.

Does the homestead exemption end when the owner dies?

Not right away. It continues for the year of death and the next tax year while the home remains part of the estate, then the new owner must reapply.

Can a cash buyer purchase an inherited house?

Yes, as long as the seller has legal authority to sign. We buy houses as they are, and we review the property and the estate paperwork before making an offer.
